---
title: "Design decisions"
---


Each of these could reasonably have gone the other way. They are written down
because the reasoning is the part that gets lost, and because anyone changing
the code deserves to know which choices are load-bearing.

## Failing on an unknown version

**Decided:** refuse a newer exchange version; read older ones.

The alternative is to read what you can and ignore the rest. That works right
up to the release where a column changes meaning rather than name, and then it
produces numbers that look fine. Since these numbers end up in publications,
the failure mode has to be loud.

## Uncoded segments are opt-in, not automatic

**Decided:** `units()` only includes segments no coder coded when the caller
passes the `uncoded` export.

Including them silently would be defensible; it is usually the methodologically
right choice, but it would also mean the same call produces different
coefficients depending on which files happen to be at hand. Requiring the
second file makes the decision visible in the code, which is where a reviewer
can see it.

## Multiple coding is set aside and counted

**Decided:** a coder's several codes on one segment make that cell missing;
the count is reported as `multi_set_aside`.

Three alternatives were considered: pick the first code (arbitrary), treat the
set as one compound category (invents categories nobody defined), or refuse to
compute anything (unhelpful). Setting aside and counting is the only option
that neither invents data nor hides how much was dropped. The per-code binary
view exists for projects where multiple coding is the norm.

## Inertia share relative to the whole table

**Decided:** `ca().inertia_share` divides by total inertia, not by the
retained dimensions.

Normalising to the retained dimensions is common and always sums to 100 %,
which reads as *this map shows everything*. The R twin had this bug, and the
cross-language comparison found it. The check that pins it down is that total
inertia must equal the chi-squared statistic over *n*.

## Monte Carlo instead of exact for large tables

**Decided:** exact Fisher only for two-by-two; permutation-based Monte Carlo
with fixed margins beyond that, seeded.

The exact test for an r-by-c table is only feasible for small counts. Six
codes over five documents with a few hundred codings is already enough to
exhaust the workspace of a standard implementation; the R twin aborted on
exactly that. Table dimensions do not predict the cost; the counts do. So
anything past two-by-two goes to simulation, and the seed makes the reported
p-value reproducible.

## Distribution name

**Decided:** the distribution is `qdaPy`, normalised by PyPI to `qdapy`, which
is also the import name.

An earlier iteration used `qda-p` with import name `qdap`, because `qdap` was
taken on PyPI by an unrelated project. `qdapy` turned out to be free, and `Py`
is the conventional suffix anyway, so the hyphen was dropped.

## No GPL dependencies

**Decided:** keep the dependency set permissive (BSD, MIT, PSF).

A copyleft dependency binds everyone downstream, so the bar for adding one is
high. Correspondence analysis is computed here from a singular value
decomposition rather than by pulling in a GPL library, which also makes it
independent of the R twin's `MASS` dependency, so the two implementations check
each other rather than sharing a code path.

Adding a dependency is therefore a licensing decision as well as a technical
one.

## One function per equation

`unitizing_alpha` used to be one long function. It is now four, and the split
follows the paper rather than a line count: `_pair_disorder` is equation (16)
for one pair of coders, `_observed_disorder` is (17) summing over pairs,
`_expected_disorder` is (18), and `unitizing_alpha` combines them into (19).

**The same split exists in qdaR and in qdaZ's `stats.js`**, with the same
boundaries and matching names. That is the point: the three can still be read
side by side against Krippendorff, which is the only practical way to check
that three languages implement one formula. Splitting one of them alone would
have bought a metric and cost the thing the metric was meant to protect.

Before and after, the two implementations were run over the same eighty random
configurations in all three languages and compared: identical to the last bit.
